title: Large areas produce more, faster-forming and wider-spreading new species

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Large areas produce more, faster-forming and wider-spreading new species

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Although small isolated areas can favour new species, modification is generally faster on large areas, and forms produced there, having beaten many competitors, spread most widely and give rise to the most new varieties and species.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Finally, I conclude that, although small isolated areas probably have been in some respects highly favourable for the production of new species, yet that the course of modification will generally have been more rapid on large areas; and what is more important, that the new forms produced on large areas, which already have been victorious over many competitors, will be those that will spread most widely

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals”. Scope: terrestrial species in continents versus islands and small regions

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-15: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Global occurrence and phylogenetic data allow broad comparative tests of each component. They do not cleanly isolate area from correlated environmental and historical causes.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare speciation, trait-evolution and geographic spread rates of lineages occupying large continental areas versus small islands or regions under phylogenetic models. Faster modification, more descendant taxa and broader later ranges from large areas support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Survivorship obscures where extinct forms originated.

Area, isolation, habitat diversity and sampling intensity are strongly confounded.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.61
discriminating power: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.66
data existence: 0.78

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Range, area, and diversification rate can be assembled from public phylogenies and occurrence or flora databases for major terrestrial groups. Small isolated areas and large continents differ in age and sampling, so a higher continental rate is not a clean reading of faster modification. The analysis can test a restricted biogeographic proxy and would take substantial harmonization of origins and clade ages.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare speciation rate, geographic range, and richness of descendant clades between lineages inferred to have originated on large landmasses and those from islands or small regions. Faster diversification and wider ranges for large-area clades would support the claim; equal or higher rates for small-area clades, after clade age and sampling effort, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Vertebrates and plants are far better covered than terrestrial invertebrates.

Area, island age, isolation, and collecting effort are entangled.

The place of origin of a clade is often ambiguous once it has spread.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.48
operationalizability: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.5
analysis feasibility: 0.62
